newsitem.title: JAPAN: Activist's death puts Japan in diplomatic quagmire.
newsitem.headline: Activist's death puts Japan in diplomatic quagmire.

text.p: Japan was plunged into a diplomatic quagmire on Thursday over a chain of disputed island in the East China Sea after an activist from a Hong Kong ship jumped overboard to his death in waters near the islands.

Despite the first death in connection with a simmering sovereignty dispute over the small uninhabited islands, Japan has no alternative to its current stance of claiming ownership of the islands and waiting for the protests to calm down, political analysts said.

Group leader David Chan died soon after jumping into rough seas from a chartered Hong Kong vessel to protest against Japan's claim to the islands, called the Senkakus in Japan and the Diaoyus in Chinese.
"There is no effective diplomatic step Japan could take to quell the emotion-filled protests," said Nozomu Akizuki of Tokai University near Tokyo.

The long-dormant dispute over the islands erupted in July after Japanese right-wingers erected a makeshift lighthouse on one of them, sparking anti-Japanese protests in Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and Macau.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda tried to calm the affair when he told his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen at the United Nations in New York on Wednesday that Tokyo would not let Japanese right-wingers take further action on the islands.
Apart from Japan's wartime aggression, anti-Japanese sentiment among Chinese and people of Chinese descent stems from a long history of troubled Sino-Japanese relations, Akizuki said.
He said Chinese people were obsessed with their traditional view that their culture was far superior to that of Japan.
"But Japan, the wartime aggressor in China, is now more advanced on the economic front. That's not what China wants," he said.
Akio Watanabe of Aoyama Gakuin University in Tokyo said there was no prospect of the dispute being settled in the near future.
He said the only possible solution could be that the countries concerned would jointly control and develop the islands for their mutual benefit.
The territorial dispute had escalated to boiling point because of a lack of diplomatic skills on the part of Japan, political analyst Minoru Morita said.
"The Senkaku problem has pushed Japan into a diplomatic crisis," he said.
He warned that the dispute could spread further to affect Japanese companies operating in China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
"Japan must seriously consider the possibility of Japanese companies being kicked out of the countries concerned," he said.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
The Taiwan government also claims ownership of the islands, saying they are under the jurisdiction of the northeastern Taiwanese county of Ilan.

Japan was given control of the islands in 1972 by the United States, which had administered the islands along with Okinawa since the end of World War Two. But the U.S. government at the time said any outstanding territorial issue should be settled among the countries concerned.
